entry: Colorless, highly volatile [[Organic compound|organic compound]] of the ether class, (CH₃CH₂)₂O. It is a common solvent and was formerly used as a general anesthetic. Valerius Cordus synthesized it in 1540 by distilling [[Ethanol|ethanol]] with [[Sulfuric acid|sulfuric acid]]. William T. G. Morton publicly demonstrated its use as an anesthetic in [[Boston]] on October 16, 1846, though Crawford Williamson Long had used it privately as early as 1842. Growing use of electrical cauterization in surgery required a switch to non-flammable anesthetics in the mid-20th century, and ether is rarely used in the 21st century.

German lyric baritone and conductor of classical music. He was best known as an interpreter of [[Franz Schubert|Schubert]]'s *Lieder*, particularly *Winterreise*, and recorded repertoire spanning centuries in several languages. Drafted into the [[Wehrmacht]] in 1943, he was captured in Italy in 1945 and spent two years as an American [[Prisoner of war|prisoner of war]], singing *Lieder* to homesick German soldiers in POW camps. He gave his first *Lieder* recital in [[Leipzig]] in 1947 and in 1948 was engaged as principal lyric baritone at the Städtische Oper Berlin. He dominated the opera and concert platforms for more than thirty years. A 1999 critics' poll ranked him the second greatest singer of the century, after Jussi Björling. He retired from the operatic stage in 1978, continued as a conductor and teacher from 1983, and made hundreds of recordings.

Subfield of [[Calculus|calculus]] concerned with the rates at which quantities change. Its primary objects are the [[Derivative|derivative]] of a [[Function (mathematics)|function]], related notions such as the differential, and their applications. The derivative at a chosen input is the instantaneous rate of change of the function there, and geometrically it is the slope of the tangent line to the graph. Finding a derivative is called differentiation. Differential and integral calculus are the two traditional divisions of calculus, connected by the [[Fundamental theorem of calculus|fundamental theorem of calculus]]. Differentiation has applications across the quantitative disciplines: the derivative of position is [[Velocity|velocity]], and the derivative of velocity is [[Acceleration|acceleration]]. Derivatives are also used to find the maxima and minima of functions.

Equation relating one or more unknown functions and their [[Derivative|derivatives]]. In applications the functions generally represent physical quantities, the derivatives represent their rates of change, and the equation defines a relationship between the two. Such equations are central to mathematical models and scientific laws in [[Physics|physics]], engineering, economics and biology. Only the simplest can be solved by explicit formulas, so solutions are often approximated numerically, while the theory of [[Dynamical system|dynamical systems]] studies their qualitative behavior. In his 1671 work, [[Isaac Newton]] listed three kinds. [[Jacob Bernoulli]] proposed the Bernoulli equation in 1695. In 1746 [[Jean Le Rond d'Alembert|Jean le Rond d'Alembert]] discovered the one-dimensional [[Wave equation|wave equation]], and in 1822 Joseph Fourier published his [[Heat equation|heat equation]] in *Théorie analytique de la chaleur*.

Branch of [[Mathematics|mathematics]] concerned with smooth shapes and spaces, known as [[Manifold|smooth manifolds]]. It uses the techniques of vector calculus, linear algebra and multilinear algebra. Its origins lie in the study of spherical geometry in antiquity, and it relates to astronomy, the geodesy of the Earth and the hyperbolic geometry of Lobachevsky. [[Eratosthenes]] calculated the circumference of the Earth around 200 BC. The simplest examples are plane and space curves and surfaces in three-dimensional [[Euclidean space|Euclidean space]], and their study formed the basis of the field in the 18th and 19th centuries. Since the late 19th century it has concerned geometric structures on differentiable manifolds, such as the distances and angles specified in [[Riemannian geometry|Riemannian geometry]]. [[Albert Einstein]] used its language in his [[General relativity|general theory of relativity]], and physicists later used it in quantum field theory and the [[Standard Model]]. It is also applied in chemistry, economics, engineering, control theory, computer graphics and machine learning.

Method of generating a shared symmetric cryptographic key over a public channel. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published it in 1976. Previously, keys had to be exchanged by physical means, such as paper key lists carried by a trusted [[Courier|courier]]. The method lets two parties with no prior contact establish a shared secret over an insecure channel. It secures many [[Internet]] services and provides forward secrecy in the ephemeral modes of [[Transport Layer Security]]. The exchange itself is not authenticated and must be combined with other protocols.

Deviation of [[Wave|waves]] from straight-line propagation, caused by an obstacle or aperture without any change in their energy. It is the same physical effect as interference, but the term diffraction is used when many waves are superposed. The resulting pattern maps the directions in which the waves travel after diffraction. Diffraction occurs for all waves, including [[Light|light]], sound, water waves, [[Gravitational wave|gravitational waves]], [[X-ray|X-rays]], radio waves, electrons and neutrons. The Italian scientist Francesco Maria Grimaldi coined the word and first recorded accurate observations of the effect in 1660. [[Thomas Young (scientist)|Thomas Young]] developed the first wave treatment in 1800, and [[Augustin-Jean Fresnel]] later devised a wave theory based on Huygens' principle. In 1818 [[Siméon Denis Poisson]] challenged Fresnel's theory by showing that it predicted light in the shadow of a circular obstruction, and Dominique-François-Jean Arago then demonstrated experimentally that such light exists.

Optical component of periodic grooves or slits, splitting light into several beams. Each beam, called a diffracted order, travels in a different direction. The angles depend on the angle of incidence, the spacing of the grooves or slits, and the wavelength of the light. Because a grating disperses light by wavelength, it is used in [[Spectrometer|spectrometers]] and monochromators. Reflective gratings have ridges on their surface, while transmissive gratings have slits. James Gregory observed diffraction patterns from a bird feather about a year after [[Isaac Newton]]'s [[Prism (optics)|prism]] experiments, effectively the first diffraction grating. The first human-made grating was made around 1785 by David Rittenhouse, who strung hairs between two finely threaded screws. Joseph von Fraunhofer, who made a wire grating in 1821, was the first to obtain line spectra with a grating. Closely spaced tracks on CDs and [[DVD|DVDs]] produce [[Rainbow|rainbow]] colors through the same effect.

Net movement of anything, such as atoms, ions, molecules or energy, from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration. It is driven by a gradient in [[Gibbs free energy|Gibbs free energy]] or chemical potential, and it can occur uphill, as in spinodal decomposition. Because particles move by random walk, diffusion mixes matter without directed bulk motion, which is the characteristic of advection; [[Convection|convection]] combines the two. Processes described by Fick's laws are called normal, or Fickian, diffusion. The word derives from [[Latin]] *diffundere*, "to spread out." As a [[Stochastic process|stochastic process]], diffusion is used in models in [[Statistics|statistics]], probability theory, information theory, neural networks, finance and marketing. In breathing, air moves into the [[Lung|lungs]] by bulk flow, and oxygen then diffuses from the alveoli into the [[Blood|blood]].

Artistic work using digital technology in its creative or presentational process. The term also covers [[Computer|computer]] art and other computational art that engages with [[Multimedia|multimedia]] or digital media. Names such as electronic art and new media art have been used since the 1960s. Digital art may be purely computer-generated, as with [[Fractal|fractals]] and algorithmic art, or may start from a scanned photograph or vector graphics. In 1974–77 [[Salvador Dalí]] made two large canvases of *Gala Contemplating the Mediterranean Sea* that appear as a portrait of [[Abraham Lincoln]] from 20 meters away. [[Andy Warhol]] created digital art on an [[Amiga]] computer, which was publicly introduced at Lincoln Center in July 1985. Digital painting imitates traditional [[Painting|painting]] with pixels on a screen, or produces physical work made with digital electronics. Artists have used artificial intelligence since at least the 1960s and generative adversarial networks since 2014.

Information represented as a string of discrete symbols, each taking one of a finite number of values from an alphabet, such as letters or digits. The most common form in modern information systems is binary data, a string of [[Bit|bits]] that each have the value 0 or 1, grouped into [[Byte|bytes]] of eight bits. It contrasts with analog data, which takes values from a continuous range, such as the air pressure variation in a [[Sound|sound]] wave. Data requires interpretation to become information. In modern computer systems all data is digital, and digital data is the main input for [[Data science|data science]], which applies methods from [[Statistics|statistics]], computer science and [[Machine learning|machine learning]]. Text is encoded with standards such as [[ASCII]]. The word digital derives from the Latin *digitus*, meaning "finger," and was used by George Stibitz of Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1942 for the fast electrical pulses of a device that aimed anti-aircraft guns.

Photography using arrays of electronic photodetectors and an analog-to-digital converter, with images stored as computer files. Digital photographs need no wet chemical processing of the kind required for [[Photographic film|photographic film]]. Most cameras have an electronic viewfinder that lets the photographer review or delete a picture within seconds, and onboard computers set focus and exposure automatically. Much of the technology originated in the space industry, where it is linked to embedded systems and remote [[Telemetry|telemetry]]. In 1957 Russell Kirsch produced the first digital image through a computer, an image of his son. The first semiconductor image sensor was the [[Charge-coupled device|charge-coupled device]], first demonstrated in April 1970. Consumer digital cameras appeared in the late 1990s, and cameras were built into [[Smartphone|cell phones]] from around 2000, particularly for their connectivity to [[Social media|social media]] and email.

Sociolinguistic arrangement of two [[Dialect|dialects]] or languages used in strictly separate settings by one community. Alongside the everyday vernacular, the *L* (low) variety, a second, highly codified *H* (high) variety serves literature, formal education and specific settings but not ordinary conversation. The *H* variety may have no native speakers. It may be an older stage of the same language, as in medieval Europe, where [[Latin]] stayed in formal use while spoken forms diverged. In northern India and Pakistan, Hindustani is used alongside [[Hindi|Hindi]] and [[Urdu|Urdu]]; other examples include Modern Standard [[Arabic]] alongside regional varieties in the [[Arab world]], and literary Tamil alongside colloquial spoken Tamil. Sociolinguist Charles A. Ferguson introduced the English term in 1959. Speakers of the *L* variety must learn the *H* variety for literacy and professional advancement, a requirement that can create educational challenges.

Right of a person to be valued and respected for their own sake and to be treated ethically. The concept is significant in [[Morality|morality]], [[Ethics|ethics]] and [[Law|law]] as an extension of Enlightenment-era ideas of inherent, inalienable rights. Contemporary dignity derives from the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]] of 1948, whose Article 1 states, "All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights." References to human dignity became more common in constitutions and charters after [[World War II]]. The English word comes from [[Latin]] *dignitas*, meaning "worthiness" or "prestige." In ordinary use it denotes respect and status, but it is rarely defined in political, legal and scientific discussions. [[Immanuel Kant]]'s principle that people should be treated as ends in themselves underlies the view that dignity forbids instrumentalizing a person. Humiliation, which diminishes a person's self-worth, is another recognized violation. Debate persists over whether dignity is an objective attribute of human beings or a relational one.

Algorithm for finding the shortest paths between nodes in a weighted graph, such as a road network. [[Edsger W. Dijkstra]] conceived it in 1956 and published it in 1959. It finds the shortest paths from a source node to every other node, and it can stop once a chosen destination is reached. It uses a min-priority queue [[Data structure|data structure]] and is normally applied to graphs with non-negative edge weights. The method underlies network routing protocols such as IS-IS and OSPF, and in [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] a variant serves as uniform cost search.

Any of four species of small [[Antelope|antelope]] in the genus *Madoqua*. They live in the bushlands of eastern and southern Africa and stand about 30–40 cm at the shoulder. Dik-diks can live up to 10 years. The name is [[Onomatopoeia|onomatopoeic]], imitating the whistled *dik* alarm call of females, which both sexes supplement with a shrill whistle that may warn other animals of predators. Dik-diks tolerate dry conditions: they have fewer sweat glands than cattle and can concentrate their urine. They usually live in pairs. [[Eagle|Eagles]] and [[Jackal|jackals]] are among their predators.

Sex toy, often explicitly phallic in form, intended for sexual penetration or other sexual activity. It is made from a variety of solid materials, and its shape and size vary widely to suit different users. The [[Oxford English Dictionary]] concluded in its third edition, published in 2018, that the word originates in nonsense syllables common in early-modern popular ballads. One of the earliest English uses it cites is in Thomas Nashe's poem "The Choise of Valentines" (c. 1593). The classical term was *olisbos*, from [[Ancient Greek]], originally a dildo usually made of leather.

Brazilian economist and politician, 36th president of Brazil (2011–16). She was the first and only woman to hold the office. She was minister of mines and energy (2003–05) and then chief of staff (2005–10) in the cabinet of [[Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva]] during his first presidency, and was elected president in 2010. Impeachment proceedings began in December 2015. On August 31, 2016, the Senate voted 61–20 to convict her of breaking budgetary laws and removed her from office, and [[Michel Temer]] succeeded her. Rousseff maintained that the proceedings were politically motivated. Since March 2023 she has chaired the New Development Bank.

Genus of theropod [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]] from the Early Jurassic, about 186 million years ago, in what is now [[North America]]. The name means "two-crested lizard," for a pair of arched crests on the [[Skull|skull]] that were probably enlarged by keratin and may have been used in visual display. Fossils from northern Arizona, collected in 1940 and 1942, were assigned to the genus in 1970. It was slender and bipedal, weighed about 400 kg (880 lb), and was among the earliest large predatory dinosaurs. In *Jurassic Park*, it was given fictional venom and an expandable neck frill.

Hindi-language romantic musical film of 1995, directed by [[Aditya Chopra]] in his directorial debut. [[Shah Rukh Khan]] and [[Kajol]] star as Raj and Simran, two non-resident Indians who fall in love during a vacation through [[Europe]]. Shot in India, [[London]] and [[Switzerland]], it was released on October 20, 1995, and was the highest-grossing Indian film of that year. It won 10 Filmfare Awards, the most for a single film at the time. It is still shown at the Maratha Mandir in [[Mumbai]] and is considered the longest-running film in the history of Indian cinema.

Minimum number of coordinates needed to specify any point in a mathematical or physical space. A line has dimension one, since a single coordinate locates a point on it, and the surface of a [[Sphere|sphere]] has dimension two, since latitude and longitude locate a point. The inside of a cube or sphere is three-dimensional. In classical mechanics, space and time are separate, but the four dimensions of [[Spacetime|spacetime]] describe events, and the pseudo-Riemannian manifolds of [[General relativity|general relativity]] describe spacetime with matter and gravity. [[String theory|Superstring theory]] uses 10 dimensions, and 11 describe supergravity and [[M-theory]]. The state space of quantum mechanics is an infinite-dimensional function space. In mathematics, dimension is the number of degrees of freedom of a point moving on an object, so a [[Tesseract|tesseract]] has dimension four and [[Euclidean space|Euclidean]] n-space has dimension n.

Colorless organosulfur compound, (CH₃)₂S=O, the most widely used commercial sulfoxide. A polar aprotic [[Solution (chemistry)|solvent]] that dissolves both polar and nonpolar compounds, it mixes with water and many organic solvents. It is made by oxidizing dimethyl sulfide, a by-product of the kraft process. After skin absorption it is metabolized to compounds that leave a [[Garlic|garlic]]-like taste in the mouth. Promoted in the 1960s for [[Analgesic|analgesic]] and anti-inflammatory effects, it is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for symptomatic relief of interstitial cystitis, and studies found limited efficacy beyond that use.

Extinct genus of carnivorous synapsids of the [[Permian]] period, known for a large sail on its back. The sail was formed by elongated spines extending from the vertebrae. It was an obligate quadruped with a tall skull and large teeth of different sizes. Most species weighed 28–250 kg. Most fossils come from the Red Beds of [[Texas]] and [[Oklahoma]], though remains have also been found in Germany, and more than a dozen species have been named since the genus was erected in 1878. Often mistaken for a [[Dinosaur|dinosaur]], it became extinct some 40 million years before dinosaurs appeared. Although reptile-like, it is more closely related to [[Mammal|mammals]] than to reptiles. It was probably an [[Apex predator|apex predator]], feeding on fish and tetrapods. The sail has been proposed as an aid to [[Thermoregulation|thermoregulation]], but some studies argue that heat regulation was not its main purpose, and courtship display is considered the most likely use.

Indian actress known mainly for Hindi films. Raised in [[Mumbai]], she was discovered at 14 by [[Raj Kapoor]], who cast her in the title role of *Bobby* (1973). She had married the actor [[Rajesh Khanna]] shortly before the film's release and quit acting. She returned to films in 1984, and her comeback film *Saagar* (1985) revived her career. She won Filmfare Awards for Best Actress for both *Bobby* and *Saagar*, and the National Film Award for Best Actress for *Rudaali* (1993). From the mid-1990s she was more selective, finding greater success in character roles, including in *Tenet* (2020), directed by [[Christopher Nolan]].

Medium-sized, lean [[Dog|dog]] lineage found in Australia, adapted for speed, agility and stamina. Its coat is light ginger or tan, black and tan, or creamy white, and its skull is wedge-shaped. Its taxonomic classification is debated: it has been treated as a form of domestic dog, as a subspecies of dog or [[Wolf|wolf]], or as a full species, *Canis dingo*. Its lineage split early from that of domestic dogs, and it is closely related to the New Guinea singing dog. Dingoes were present in Australia more than 3,000 years ago. The name comes from the Dharug language of the [[Sydney]] area. A pack usually consists of a mated pair, their offspring from the current year and sometimes the previous year. As mainland Australia's [[Apex predator|apex predator]], it preys on [[Red fox|red foxes]] and feral cats. Genetic studies show minimal contemporary [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridization]] with domestic dogs. Well-known populations live on K'gari in [[Queensland]], and the dingo is listed as vulnerable in some jurisdictions, including [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]].
